data.title: Credentials Committed to Source Control
data.summary: Working credentials were present in source repositories, including in historical commits. Removing a secret in a later commit does not remove it from history, so anyone who can clone the repository can recover it.
data.description:
Secrets reach repositories through configuration committed for convenience, test fixtures using real credentials, and debugging changes that were never reverted. The usual remediation — deleting the line and committing — leaves the value in history, where it is trivially recovered.

Public repositories are scanned continuously by third parties, and exposure is measured in minutes. Private repositories are not safe either: they are cloned onto laptops, mirrored into CI, and become readable to everyone who ever had access, including departed staff and compromised contractor accounts.

Developer forks and local clones mean that even a deleted repository may persist elsewhere.
data.recommendation:
* Treat any committed secret as compromised and rotate it immediately; purging history is cleanup, not remediation.
* Run secret scanning on every push, and block commits that introduce credentials.
* Keep configuration out of code, loading secrets from the environment or a secrets manager.
* Scan existing history across all repositories, including archived ones and forks.
data.short_recommendation: Rotate exposed secrets and scan commits before they land.
